prize_parts.citation: for incorporating electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity into formal and empirical analysis of fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: After reading the openings I still rank B006 first on the common criteria. The discovery is conceptual and general. Constitutions, electoral rules, accountability and state capacity became endogenous objects of analysis, and government stopped being treated as a benevolent planner. The work joined formal theory to comparative empirical tests and then shaped later work in public finance, development and growth. It also connects to long-run questions of institutional persistence and state building that economic historians take seriously, which is why I do not rank it on field affinity alone. Attribution is relatively clean for this field. Persson and Tabellini are the central pair for the constitutional and electoral-rule programme and its synthesis, and Besley's accountability and state-capacity work, partly joint with Persson, is a distinct, closely related strand. Maturity is not a concern, because the core work is 20 to 30 years old and has been built on extensively. B001 has the broadest opening support (ten top-three placements) and very large practical influence. I judge its three-name attribution to be less clean, and that is the main reason I keep B006 ahead of it.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity covers adjacent ground, so the Committee may see a closely related institutional prize as too soon. The second is identification. The theory is strong, but the cross-country evidence on constitutional effects rests on observational variation and is contested. The third is scope: the discovery description is broad, and any three names drawn from political economics leave out comparable contributors, or contributors already recognised. B001 has stronger breadth of support and policy reach than B006, and the Committee could reasonably weigh that more heavily than I do.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B001 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He finds the framework foundational with decades of use, but concedes that choosing three from a crowded field is contestable. He ranks B006 second, as a clean trio, and flags the 2024 prize as a possible brake.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of both candidates, and it is why I weigh attribution so heavily. B001's influence on central-bank practice is hard to dispute, but his own caveats (a trio that could shift toward Gali or Gertler, Gertler's overlap with B002, post-2008 and post-2021 performance debates) are all attribution or durability concerns. B006 has fewer of them. I share his worry about the 2024 prize but would qualify it. That prize rewarded a specific historical-institutional mechanism, whereas this work concerns how formal political rules map into fiscal and policy outcomes. The two are neighbours, not substitutes. I accept that a Committee could still treat the neighbouring status as decisive.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 fourth with only Persson and Tabellini. He credits them with the core programme and synthesis. He calls excluding Besley a difficult judgement and notes the proximity of the 2024 institutions prize.
responses.response: I take the Besley question seriously, and a two-person prize is a defensible alternative. I keep Besley because state capacity and political agency are a separate achievement from the constitutional and electoral-rule programme, and the three-person limit allows for him. Dropping him would narrow the citation to electoral rules and constitutions and understate the accountability and state-capacity strand, which links most directly to the long-run historical literature. If the Committee finds Besley's claim less separable from Persson's joint work than I do, the Persson-Tabellini pair would be the natural fallback.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B006 sixth. He treats the work as a rigorous synthesis with a clear and well-matched attribution, but says causal identification in the constitutional-effects work is harder than in more design-based fields.
responses.response: I agree on identification and do not want to oversell the cross-country empirics. Where I differ is in what the discovery is. The lasting contribution is the formal-plus-empirical framework that made institutional design analysable, and the individual coefficient estimates matter less. Weaker identification affects some conclusions and leaves the conceptual advance standing. It does mean the citation should be worded around the framework and the analysis of policy outcomes, not around settled causal effects of particular constitutions, and I have drafted it that way.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first and B006 second. He describes B006 as a systematic, empirically testable theory that turned a loose field into mainstream economics, a mature case and arguably overdue. He discloses an IIES proximity to Persson.
responses.response: I agree with the maturity and coherence argument. I would not rest anything on 'overdue', because time elapsed is not scientific merit. The case stands on breadth of application, a clean attribution and decades of confirmation. I note his disclosed proximity to Persson, which I am not adjudicating. Where we differ is on B001 versus B006 as the lead. His own B001 caveats (crowded credit, the empirical weakness of the Phillips curve and the role of heterogeneity) reinforce my concern about how cleanly three names can carry that discovery.

uncertainties: How far the 2024 institutions prize should reduce the Committee's willingness to reward B006, and whether the topics are neighbouring or overlapping.
Whether Besley's state-capacity and accountability work is separable enough from the joint work with Persson to justify a third laureate.
How much weight the contested cross-country identification of constitutional effects should carry relative to the conceptual contribution.

Whether B001's broader opening support reflects a stronger case on the common criteria, or only the diffuseness of the field. That depends on how a three-person attribution (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) is judged against Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets.
My assessments rest on general knowledge and the supplied ballot text, not on independent verification of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the candidates or credited names in B006, B001 or B020. I note, for transparency only, that I am at Lund and have worked with the political scientist Johannes Lindvall on railroads and political reform. That is adjacent to the political-economy field but not to the named candidates. I am also a Lund colleague of Tommy Andersson and Jan Teorell was formerly at Lund; neither relationship concerns the candidate work.
